learn.title: Finding the Best Wind Sites
learn.intro: Wind resource assessment is the first step in building profitable wind farms. Developers measure wind speed, direction, and turbulence over months or years to predict energy output. Accurate data prevents costly mistakes and ensures projects deliver reliable clean energy for decades.
learn.c1_text: Advanced software models wind flow across terrain using computational fluid dynamics. These tools simulate how hills, forests, and buildings affect wind speed. This helps estimate annual energy production before construction begins.
learn.c3_text: India ranks 4th globally in wind capacity with over 44 GW installed by 2023. The Tamil Nadu coast and Gujarat offer some of the best wind resources, contributing significantly to the country’s renewable energy targets.
learn.stat2: Global potential: 22,000 GW of economically viable wind (IRENA)
learn.stat3: Typical wind farm requires 6–12 months of site data collection
learn.stat4: Modern turbines can capture wind at speeds up to 25 m/s

learn.title: India's EV Policy Framework
learn.intro: India's electric vehicle policies aim to reduce oil imports and curb urban air pollution. With ambitious electrification targets, the government offers subsidies and incentives through schemes like PM e-DRIVE, shaping the future of mobility in one of the world's largest auto markets.
learn.c1_text: Launched in 2019, PM e-DRIVE provides demand-side incentives for electric buses, cars, and two-wheelers. It supports charging infrastructure and aims to accelerate EV adoption. Think of it as a subsidy bridge helping buyers switch from petrol to cleaner options.
learn.c2_text: States like Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu have introduced their own EV policies offering road tax waivers, registration benefits, and local manufacturing incentives. These complement central schemes and tailor solutions to regional needs.
learn.c3_text: As of 2023, India has over 1.4 million registered EVs. The FAME scheme has supported more than 1.1 million EV purchases since launch. Government targets 30% vehicle electrification by 2030 to cut emissions and fuel costs.
learn.stat1: Over 1.4 million EVs registered in India (2023)
learn.stat2: FAME scheme supported 1.1 million+ EV purchases since inception
learn.stat4: Over 120,000 public EV charging points installed under government programs

learn.title: Harvesting Energy from Ocean Waves
learn.intro: Wave energy converters transform the rhythmic motion of ocean waves into usable electricity. Unlike solar or wind, wave energy is highly predictable and dense, offering a consistent power source. Though still emerging, it holds vast potential for coastal nations.
learn.c1_text: These devices use wave action to compress air in a chamber, driving a turbine. Imagine blowing across a bottle top—the moving air spins a turbine inside. OWCs are robust and work well in moderate wave climates.
learn.c2_text: Point absorbers bob up and down on wave crests, while attenuators flex along their length. Both convert kinetic motion into mechanical energy via hydraulic pistons or generators. They’re like buoys dancing to the ocean’s beat.
learn.c3_text: India has identified 300 GW potential in ocean energy. The National Institute of Ocean Technology leads pilot projects along the Andaman coast. With strong monsoon waves, India is well-positioned to harness this untapped resource.
learn.stat2: India's identified ocean energy potential: 300 GW
learn.stat3: A single 1 MW wave device can power ~750 homes annually
learn.stat4: Over 200 wave energy converter prototypes tested worldwide

learn.title: Using Earth's Heat for Power
learn.intro: Geothermal energy taps into Earth’s internal heat for electricity and heating. Unlike solar or wind, it provides baseload power—available 24/7. It’s especially valuable in tectonically active regions, offering a stable, low-carbon alternative to fossil fuels.
learn.c1_text: Hot water or steam from underground reservoirs drives turbines connected to generators. Picture a kettle boiling continuously beneath your feet—the Earth naturally heats fluid that rises to spin machinery above ground.
learn.c2_text: In areas without natural reservoirs, engineers inject water into hot dry rock to create artificial ones. This expands geothermal reach beyond volcanic zones. It’s like fracking for heat—creating pathways where none existed before.
learn.c3_text: India has 10 geothermal provinces, including the Himalayas and Andaman Islands. The government plans to add 10 GW of geothermal capacity by 2030. Pilot projects in Ladakh and Assam are exploring local applications for heating and power.
learn.stat3: Geothermal plants operate at 90% capacity factor vs. 25% for solar
learn.stat4: Target: India aims for 10 GW geothermal by 2030

learn.title: Boosting Solar Manufacturing in India
learn.intro: India's Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme strengthens domestic solar manufacturing to reduce import dependence. By supporting large-scale production, India aims to become a global solar hub while creating jobs and ensuring affordable clean energy access.
learn.c1_text: The PLI scheme allocates ₹19,500 crore to incentivize solar module manufacturing. Companies receive financial rewards based on sales volume. Think of it as a performance bonus encouraging factories to produce more high-efficiency panels locally.
learn.c2_text: To qualify, manufacturers must use a minimum percentage of locally sourced materials. This builds supply chains within India, reducing reliance on imports—especially from China. It’s like nurturing homegrown tech instead of buying everything abroad.
learn.c3_text: Under PLI, over 20 GW of solar manufacturing capacity is being set up. Reliance, Adani, and others are building gigafactories. This supports India's 500 GW non-fossil fuel target by 2030 and creates thousands of jobs in clean energy.
learn.stat2: Over 20 GW of solar manufacturing capacity under development
learn.stat3: India's solar target: 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030
learn.stat4: China currently supplies ~80% of global solar modules

learn.title: How Solar Panels Generate Electricity
learn.intro: Solar photovoltaic (PV) panels convert sunlight directly into electricity using the photoelectric effect. Discovered by Einstein, this process powers homes, businesses, and grids worldwide. Understanding it is key to embracing solar as a core part of the clean energy transition.
learn.c1_text: When photons hit semiconductor material in solar cells, they knock electrons loose, generating electric current. Think of sunlight as tiny billiard balls knocking marbles off a board—the freed electrons flow through wires to make electricity.
learn.c2_text: Most panels use crystalline silicon, which absorbs photons effectively. Typical efficiency ranges from 15–22%, meaning only part of sunlight becomes electricity. Higher-end panels use rare materials to boost performance but cost more.
learn.c3_text: India has installed over 70 GW of solar power by 2024, making it one of the world’s fastest-growing solar markets. Large parks like Bhadla in Rajasthan rank among the largest solar installations globally, powering millions of homes.
learn.stat3: One million solar panels generate ~250 MW enough for 75,000 homes
learn.stat4: Global solar generation grew 25% annually in last five years (IEA)
